briefing: Trump says the Iran war will end very soon, either through a deal or by force, while Iran's two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz still waits on a U.S. answer and oil stays above US$110. Americans vote Tuesday after Trump closed his weekend in Kansas, where a Democrat leads recent Senate polls. In Ontario, retailers want the province's new powers against illegal cannabis stores to come with real enforcement.
headline: Trump says Iran war will end 'one way or the other' as vote nears

keyDates.label: U.S. midterm elections
keyDates.why: Control of Congress decides how much room Trump has on tariffs and the Iran war.

keyDates.why: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables 'Masters of Our Destiny', a budget themed on economic sovereignty.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran responded by choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened the strait, but it collapsed in July and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Yemen's Houthis have since widened the fight with missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Egypt's parliament has authorized sending troops to help the Saudis. Qatar handed Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25, which Tehran said contained ideas it could not accept.
stories.headline: Trump says Iran war will end 'one way or the other' as Hormuz plan waits
stories.impact: Expect GTA gas and diesel prices to stay high, which feeds into grocery, delivery and transit costs. Alberta oil revenues rise, but Ontario households and manufacturers mostly feel the cost side.
stories.now: Trump said the war will be over very soon, one way or the other, telling Tehran it can make a deal or the U.S. will finish it; he has pledged no new strikes before Tuesday's midterms. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Qatar's mediators cut the reopening window in their plan from five days to two, but there is no breakthrough and the outcome depends on Washington; Iran's conditions include lifting sanctions, releasing frozen funds and a smaller U.S. military presence. Iran's army spokesman warned that a new war could last longer than the last one, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards say more tankers have caught fire after hitting mines in the strait, which could not be independently verified. U.S. Central Command says its blockade has turned back 144 vessels, and Brent crude ended October at US$113.43 a barrel.

stories.summary: Trump warned that the war will end very soon either through a deal or by force, while Iran's talks with Qatari mediators on a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz still hinge on Washington's reply.

stories.why: Oil above US$110 is the main force behind higher inflation in Canada and the U.S., and it pushed the Bank of Canada into a rate hike this week. A real reopening plan could pull prices down quickly, while a collapse of talks could send them higher.

stories.backstory: Broad Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, and Trump then imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian counter-tariffs. Since then the White House has repeatedly adjusted which products are covered, easing some farm and forestry goods while adding others. Separate U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos under a national-security law (Section 232) hit Ontario's factories hardest. Sources said this week a narrower deal on steel and autos was possible before the midterms, but U.S. officials want more concessions.
stories.headline: Carney reports 'good conversation' with Trump as trade teams keep talking
stories.impact: Factory jobs in Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and the GTA's parts plants remain exposed. Some imported goods such as paint, rugs and air conditioners may cost more if Canada responds or suppliers pass on costs.
stories.now: In a post on X on Sunday, Carney said his conversation with Trump built on recent constructive talks about a trade deal and that negotiators will work toward one over the coming weeks; he framed the goal as protecting jobs, affordability and Canada's culture and sovereignty. No tariff relief or timeline was announced. On Oct. 30 the U.S. reshuffled its list of Canadian goods facing 50% tariffs, dropping items like plywood and cardboard boxes and adding paint, carpets and air conditioners, and Trump has said steel and auto tariffs on Canada will rise to 50% on Jan. 1. Ottawa is also courting other partners, with a Carney trip to Antigua and Barbuda Nov. 2–4 and a possible India deal before Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits Dec. 11–12. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says Canadians need results, not signing ceremonies.

stories.why: Ontario sells most of its steel and auto output to the U.S., and the province says steel exports there have fallen by more than half since 2024. The midterm result could change how willing Washington is to bargain.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers of Congress since January 2025. All 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate are on the ballot on Nov. 3. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war have hurt Trump's approval, which Reuters recently put at 32%. Recent national polls have given Democrats a lead on the generic ballot.
stories.headline: Trump closes in Kansas as Democrats lead most key Senate polls
stories.impact: The outcome will shape U.S. tariff policy on Canadian steel and autos and the timing of any strikes on Iran, both of which affect Ontario jobs and fuel prices.
stories.now: A University of Florida Election Lab count put early ballots at 53.1 million on Sunday, about 29 million in person and 23 million by mail, compared with roughly 46 million early votes in 2022. Trump rallied in Dubuque, Iowa, Sunday afternoon and then at Salina's airport in the evening for Marshall, after first cancelling the Kansas trip. New YouGov polls published Sunday show Democrats narrowly ahead in Kansas (50% to 49%), Texas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Iowa, with Nebraska tied, most within the margin of error. An Emerson College poll from Oct. 26–28 had Hamilton at 48.7% and Marshall at 45.2% in a state Trump won by about 16 points in 2024.

stories.summary: More than 53 million Americans voted early, and Trump ended his weekend with a Sunday evening rally in Salina, Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton leads recent polls against Sen. Roger Marshall.

stories.why: A Democratic Congress could check Trump's tariffs and war powers, while Republican control would give him a freer hand for the next two years.

stories.backstory: The Bank of Canada cut to 2.25% in October 2025 and then held for seven meetings. Oil prices driven up by the Iran war lifted September inflation to 3.1%, even as Canada lost 68,000 jobs that month. The bank's new forecast puts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, well above its 2% target. Flat growth and rising rates together raise the risk of stagflation, meaning weak growth with high inflation.
stories.headline: Economy stalls in August, two days after Bank of Canada's hike
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit already cost more after the hike. A weak economy could slow hiring in the GTA, so it is a good moment to review budgets and renewal plans.
stories.now: Real gross domestic product (GDP) was unchanged in August, missing the 0.2% gain economists expected, with retail up 1.2% but wholesale trade and car-and-parts manufacturing down. StatCan's early estimate shows a 0.1% drop in September as manufacturing and oil and gas output fell, leaving third-quarter growth at about 0.3%. That follows Wednesday's quarter-point hike to 2.50%, which the Bank of Canada made to keep high oil prices from spreading through the economy, while signalling more could be needed. Premier Doug Ford called the hike a massive mistake, and Ontario's fall update now sees provincial growth of only 0.5% this year.

stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the economy was flat in August and probably shrank 0.1% in September, a weak backdrop for the Bank of Canada's first rate increase since 2023.

August GDP flat; September seen down 0.1%

stories.why: The data shows the bank raising rates into a stalling economy, a tough trade-off that makes its next moves less predictable.

stories.backstory: Michigan's Senate seat is open because Democrat Gary Peters is retiring, and it is one of the closest races that will decide which party controls the Senate. El-Sayed, a former public health official who would be the first Muslim U.S. senator, narrowly beat Stevens in the August Democratic primary even though she had strong backing from the party's Senate campaign arm. Rogers is a former Republican congressman who narrowly lost the state's 2024 Senate race. Early voting in Michigan began Oct. 24.
stories.headline: Democrat Haley Stevens appears with GOP's Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
stories.impact: Michigan is Ontario's biggest cross-border auto partner, and the Senate's makeup will shape how much room Trump has on tariffs that hit plants in Windsor, Oshawa and Alliston.
stories.now: On Sunday morning Stevens attended a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit with Rogers and his wife, saying in brief remarks that Rogers would back investment in Black-owned businesses; Rogers called her a courageous leader. She had been due at a Democratic unity event with Rep. Jim Clyburn, but Rep. Debbie Dingell said she asked Stevens to stay away after the feud became too distracting, then cancelled the event. The split began when Stevens demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad tying U.S. military aid to Israel to grocery prices, which she called antisemitic; El-Sayed says he did not make the ad and disagrees with it. Stevens has said she still backs the Democratic ticket, while her fiancé says he will vote for Rogers.

stories.backstory: Ontario's spring budget had already run deeper deficits as U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos hit the province's factories. The Ford government has said it will spend through the trade war rather than cut sharply. Ottawa and Ontario have also announced a joint $8.7-billion plan to support steel and auto manufacturing.
stories.headline: Ontario's deficit swells to $16.9 billion as tariffs delay balanced budget
stories.impact: Buyers of new homes may get a tax break, and business owners can write off equipment faster. The province says health spending rises, but a hiring freeze and payment reviews are part of its savings plan.
stories.now: The Oct. 29 update puts this year's deficit 22% above the spring plan, partly because of a roughly $3.8-billion top-up to a contingency fund for tariff costs. Next year's shortfall more than doubles to $12.7 billion from $6.1 billion, and 2028 now shows a $6.7-billion deficit instead of balance. Ontario will match Ottawa's 100% write-off for business investment, an $8-billion tax cut over five years the province says could create up to 30,000 jobs, and adds a tax break for buyers of newly built homes. Interest on provincial debt costs $17.4 billion this year.

stories.summary: Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy's fall economic statement projects a record $16.9-billion deficit this year and $36 billion over three years, pushing a balanced budget beyond 2028.

timeline.event: Ontario budget delays balance amid tariffs

stories.why: Bigger deficits mean more provincial borrowing and interest costs, which can squeeze future spending on health, schools and transit.

stories.backstory: The energy board resets regulated prices every Nov. 1 and May 1 based on forecast supply costs. Winter time-of-use hours shift so the expensive on-peak periods fall on weekday mornings and early evenings, when heating and lighting demand is highest. The provincial rebate is a taxpayer-funded discount shown on bills, and the province adjusts its size when underlying prices move. Most GTA homes are on time-of-use pricing unless they opted for tiered or ultra-low overnight plans.
stories.headline: Ontario hydro rates drop as winter pricing kicks in
stories.impact: Lower per-kWh prices are partly offset by a smaller rebate, so actual bills depend on usage and your utility. Ultra-low overnight customers who run appliances between 4 and 9 p.m. on weekdays face the highest rate in the province.
stories.now: The Ontario Energy Board's winter time-of-use prices are now 9.1 cents per kilowatt-hour off-peak, 14.6 cents mid-peak and 18.9 cents on-peak. Ultra-low overnight customers pay 3.7 cents from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. but 37.7 cents on weekday evenings from 4 to 9 p.m. Tiered customers pay 11.2 cents for the first 1,000 kWh a month and 13.2 cents above that. The Ontario Electricity Rebate drops to 15.7%, which the board says still trims about $23 a month from a typical 700 kWh household bill.

sources.title: Ontario Energy Board: Changes to electricity prices

stories.summary: New regulated electricity prices took effect Nov. 1, lower than a year ago, while the provincial rebate on bills shrinks to 15.7%.
stories.why: Electricity is a fixed monthly cost for every household, and the rate structure rewards shifting laundry, dishwashers and EV charging to off-peak hours.

stories.backstory: By-elections fill House of Commons seats left empty between general elections. Two of the Quebec seats emptied when NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice and Bloc MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay left to run, successfully, in Quebec's 2026 provincial election. Steven Guilbeault resigned his seat in August, and Saskatchewan Conservative Cathay Wagantall resigned on Aug. 31. The prime minister has discretion over when to call by-elections within legal time limits.
stories.headline: Carney calls six federal by-elections for Dec. 7, including Scarborough North
stories.impact: Scarborough North residents vote on Dec. 7 and will need to check registration with Elections Canada. Ontario voters elsewhere will see the results as an early signal on federal politics ahead of the next general election.
stories.now: The Prime Minister's Office announced on Sunday that by-elections will be held Dec. 7 in Scarborough North and Brantford–Brant South in Ontario, three Quebec ridings (Laurier–Sainte-Marie, Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe–Bagot–Acton) and Yorkton–Melville in Saskatchewan. Scarborough North opened up when Liberal MP Shaun Chen stepped down for health reasons after a car crash in October 2025. In Brantford–Brant South, Conservative Larry Brock left to return to work as a Crown prosecutor; the Liberals are running Joy O'Donnell, the Conservatives former Brantford mayor Kevin Davis, and Brock's preferred successor Dave Carroll plans to run as an independent. In Laurier–Sainte-Marie, vacated by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault, the Liberals have nominated former Desjardins chief executive Guy Cormier.

stories.why: Six seats are a measurable test of Carney's government a year and a half into his mandate, in the middle of a trade war and a budget week. Results in a Scarborough Liberal seat and a Conservative-held Brantford riding will show how Ontario voters are leaning.

stories.backstory: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years as the Iran war pushed oil above US$100 a barrel. Tech giants have spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI), and those stocks have driven much of the market's swings this month. Strong U.S. growth paired with high energy prices keeps pressure on the Fed not to cut.
stories.headline: U.S. economy grows 3.4% in third quarter as inflation cools
stories.impact: Canadian fixed mortgage rates follow bond yields, so they are unlikely to fall soon. Strong U.S. demand helps Ontario exporters that are not hit by tariffs.
stories.now: The Bureau of Economic Analysis said real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, driven by business investment in equipment and computers, inventory building and consumer spending. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at a 2.1% rate, down from 5.0%, and core PCE, which excludes food and energy, eased to 2.5%. The data came a day after the Federal Reserve held its key rate at 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack favouring a hike. Gold fell to a one-year low on Friday as investors bet rates will stay high.

stories.summary: The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate from July to September, faster than the spring, while a key inflation gauge eased.

stories.why: A strong U.S. economy and a hawkish Fed tend to keep bond yields up on both sides of the border.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, and both sides now regularly strike each other's energy sites. A local humanitarian ceasefire began in occupied Oleshky in Kherson region on Oct. 27, and a Ukrainian delegation arrived there on Oct. 30. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin on Oct. 21 as Washington pushes for new talks.
stories.headline: Kherson truce ends as Russian strikes leave Ukrainians without power
stories.impact: Canada's €500-million pledge adds to federal spending ahead of Thursday's budget; the war also keeps European energy markets tight, adding to global fuel prices.
stories.now: The local Kherson ceasefire, which let civilians leave Russian-occupied Oleshky and was brokered with help from Melania Trump and Pope Leo, ended at 21:00 GMT Sunday. Overnight Russian strikes hit energy sites in four regions; most Dnipropetrovsk customers were reconnected by Sunday evening but more than 60,000 were still without power, and a strike in Vinnytsia region killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl. Kyiv faces long daily power cuts and water disruptions, and Ukraine's air alert system appeared to be hacked Sunday evening with a false radiation warning for the capital. Ukraine says it hit a major missile-fuel plant in Russia's Rostov region, and Zelensky is pressing allies for more Patriot interceptors ahead of hoped-for talks in Abu Dhabi Nov. 6–10.

stories.summary: A short humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky in Kherson region expired Sunday night, as Russian strikes on the power grid kept outages in place across Ukraine.

stories.why: Talks in early November could be the first real test of a ceasefire path since early this year.

stories.backstory: The attack drew national attention because it took place in the Bridle Path, one of Toronto's wealthiest neighbourhoods. The family's father, David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, has called the experience terrifying and urged anyone with information to come forward. Police say it was the 119th home invasion reported in Toronto this year, up about 32% from the same period in 2025. Chief Myron Demkiw promised a stronger police presence in the area.
stories.headline: Canada-wide warrant issued in Bridle Path home invasion
stories.impact: Police remain on the lookout for two more suspects in their 20s, so North York residents may see extra patrols. Police are asking anyone with information or home security video from the area to contact them.
stories.now: Police issued a Canada-wide arrest warrant on Saturday for Daijohn Richards, 23, who went to hospital later on Oct. 29 with a gunshot wound to the shoulder that police believe another suspect fired by accident. He faces charges including discharging a firearm with intent to wound, armed robbery and aggravated assault. Police say three masked men with handguns and a hammer forced their way into a Hyde Park Circle home near Bayview and Lawrence avenues around 3:45 a.m.; three of the four family members were shot and two were struck with a hammer. All four are expected to survive, though two have life-altering injuries, and police believe the home was chosen for the area's wealth rather than the family itself.

stories.summary: Toronto police have named a 23-year-old suspect who they say was shot by an accomplice during Thursday's violent home invasion, and two other suspects are still being sought.

timeline.event: Home invasion at Hyde Park Circle; four hospitalized

stories.why: Toronto home invasions are up about a third this year, and this case has raised questions about residential security across the city.

stories.backstory: The EBR, passed in 1993, gives Ontarians a formal say in environmental decisions and ways to challenge them. The Ford government has repeatedly passed omnibus bills aimed at speeding housing, mining and infrastructure, arguing U.S. tariffs make faster approvals urgent. Environment Minister Todd McCarthy says Ontario is short of landfill space, made worse by a U.S. tariff on Canadian waste-hauling trucks. The legislature only returned in late October after a 21-week break.
stories.headline: Ford's Bill 140 would cut public appeal rights to speed approvals
stories.impact: GTA communities near proposed landfills or industrial sites, such as Brampton with its Emerald waste expansion debate, could have fewer ways to object. Supporters say faster approvals could speed housing and infrastructure.
stories.now: Tabled Oct. 27 by Red Tape Reduction Minister Andrea Khanjin, Bill 140 amends 23 laws and creates two new ones. It would repeal the Environmental Bill of Rights (EBR) sections that let residents request reviews and investigations or sue to protect the environment, remove third-party appeals of some environmental approvals, and drop the rule that landfill developers need the host municipality's support. A 'shot clock' would automatically approve certain permits if the province misses its deadline. The government says the changes would cut about 220,000 days of approval time, while groups including Ecojustice, Ontario Nature and the Canadian Environmental Law Association want it withdrawn.

sources.title: The Pointer: Bill 140 and Ontario's environmental laws

stories.summary: Ontario's new omnibus 'Building Ontario Faster' bill would trim the province's Environmental Bill of Rights and make landfills easier to approve, drawing pushback from environmental groups.
stories.why: It would change how much say residents and municipalities have over landfills, permits and other projects near them.

stories.backstory: Recreational cannabis became legal in Canada in October 2018, and Ontario licenses private stores through the AGCO. Enforcement against unlicensed shops has largely fallen to police and cities, and the AGCO has not had a clear mandate to go after them. In 2024 the province set aside $31 million over three years for an OPP-led cannabis enforcement team. In January 2025 Toronto's bylaw officers stopped closing illegal dispensaries, citing a lack of funding and safety concerns.
stories.headline: Legal pot shops say Ontario's illegal-store crackdown needs real enforcement
stories.impact: If the powers pass and are funded, unlicensed storefronts in Toronto and the GTA could face inspections, seizures and fines; buyers can check the AGCO's map to confirm a store is licensed.
stories.now: The proposal, announced Oct. 19, would give the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario (AGCO) power to inspect suspected illegal stores, seize products and issue fines; no fine amounts have been released. Ministry data suggest about 30% of the province's cannabis retail market is still illegal, alongside roughly 1,800 licensed stores. A Toronto store owner told CP24 the plan has no budget or timeline yet, and the Retail Cannabis Council of Ontario says success means closures that stick. Attorney General Doug Downey says illegal sellers undermine legitimate businesses and pose risks to consumers.

sources.title: CP24: Ontario proposes crackdown on illegal cannabis stores

stories.summary: Ontario plans to let its alcohol and cannabis regulator inspect, seize from and fine illegal cannabis storefronts, and licensed retailers say the move is overdue but untested.
stories.why: Illegal stores undercut licensed shops that pay more than $10,000 in fees and face background checks, and unregulated products carry health risks.

stories.backstory: Alaska uses an open top-four primary and ranked-choice voting in general elections, so voters can rank several candidates. A judge allowed Daniel J. Sullivan onto the primary ballot over the summer, and he advanced to the general election against the senator with the same name. The Justice Department sued on Oct. 23, and Alaska's election officials asked the court to dismiss the case on Oct. 27. The seat is one of several close races that could decide Senate control.
stories.headline: Judge throws out Justice Department suit over Alaska Senate ballots
stories.impact: No direct effect in Ontario, but a cleaner count in close Senate races means a faster answer on which party will shape U.S. tariff and war policy.
stories.now: U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled Sunday in a 20-page order that the Justice Department lacked standing, because a court order could not fix the harm it claimed, and that it offered no workable way to separate ballots without breaking voter secrecy. The department had argued that a teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan was put on the ballot to confuse voters and pull support from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, helping Democrat Mary Peltola. A separate federal criminal investigation into how he got on the ballot continues, with subpoenas sent to several Democratic officials, but no one has been charged.

sources.title: CBS News: Judge tosses DOJ lawsuit over Alaska Senate race
CNN: Judge throws out DOJ attempt to delay Alaska certification
Axios: DOJ sues to block Alaska results

stories.summary: A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's bid to set aside Alaska ballots ranking a second candidate named Dan Sullivan and to hold up certification if the Republican incumbent loses.

timeline.event: Second Dan Sullivan advances from primary
State asks judge to toss the case

stories.why: It is the second court loss in days for federal attempts to intervene in state vote counts, limiting the chance of results being held up in a close Senate race.
